utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of General Subotic's statement in the English language and then I will ask the witness to answer some questions in relation to a few documents that we will be leading live. [In English] Bogdan Subotic was minister of defence of the Republika Srpska from April 1992 to February 1993. When the new government of the Serbian Republic of BH was elect on 19th of January, 1993, Bogdan Subotic was appointed chief inspector of the army and military advisor to the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska, and in May 1993, also as advisor to the decorations office of the RS President Karadzic. There are many reasons behind the outbreak of war in BH, including Alija Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration with a worked-out plan for the Islamisation of BH in the next ten years, as well as the creation of national parties with very difficult programmes in BH. The international community contributed significantly to the outbreak of armed conflict. This is especially reflected in illegal imports and procurement of weapons from other countries. In early 1992, at the beginning of the war in BH no weapons from outside came to arm the Serbs. Following the clashes between Croatian and Serbian armed forces at Plitvice in Croatia, the Croats blocked Jasenovac, and Ustashas from Croatia, the ZNG and Patriotic League and other paramilitary units, flooded BH. Bogdan Subotic decided to use all the available equipment and soldiers to block borders with the BH in areas where they had been breached in order to prevent raids by these paramilitary formations. Serbs did not make any plans before the war. Alija Izetbegovic did make plans. The Serbs made efforts in the Assembly of BH and wanted to preserve Yugoslavia. They did not have any plans about incorporating municipalities. From the outset, Muslims and Croats in Sarajevo were prepared to engage in war. The police forces were cleansed of Serbs and the illegal formations within the Patriotic League were reinforced, within the Territorial Defence and the reserve police force, there were also independent armed units. The authorities left the Serbs without any protection and allowed armed groups and formations to kill and abuse Serbs and go unpunished. Complicity in the crimes against the Serbs in Sarajevo included top authorities in BH. All decisions made by the Muslim leadership were made at meetings of the innermost SDA leadership. The media in Sarajevo, which were mostly under Muslim control, played an important role in demonising the determines, instigating war and inciting crimes against them. The international press portrayed Alija Izetbegovic and his so-called multi-cultural Bosnia as an unarmed and unexpectedly attacked victim of Serbian aggression. The Islamic religious community took an active role in the pursuit of the political objectives of the Muslims in BH as well as in the crimes against the Serbian people. Radovan Karadzic did not illegally influence or pressure the work of the government in Republika Srpska beyond the legal authorities of the President of Republika Srpska. The Crisis Staffs were created in municipalities in 1992, after the other side created theirs. This lasted until mid-1992, when the communication system was established and the Assembly took control over the municipalities. They were practically not regulated. Everyone had a difficult time, both the municipality leadership and the Territorial Defence. A temporary solution organised to prevent and anarchy. No one from the leadership was controlling the Crisis Staffs. There were no lines of communication arose to -- the Territorial Defence units were self-organised with no Supreme Command. The structure of the army was proposed by General Mladic in accordance with the law. Until the army was formed on the 12th of May, 1992, the public defended themselves. There was an agreement between Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and the authorities in Belgrade that JNA units would stay in BH as a guarantor of peace to prevent all conflicts and war, and the time discussed was five years. They secured very little. On 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka the army was created by the National Assembly. Bogdan Subotic's task was to propose a Law on Defence and the army to the government. The decision on 12th of May, 1992, stated that the defence minister was responsible to bring out all enactment and implementing legislation within three months pursuant to the law. Radovan Karadzic never made decisions without expert consultations. He always obeyed the law and never made decisions by himself. He would consult the government or the relevant minister before making a decision. He was not a soldier, and therefore when he made decisions regarding the army, he would call on the minister of defence to look at the laws and the rules so that he could make a decision which he could then pass to the Main Staff. The Main Staff initiated military operations. They would prepare a proposal for the president who would consider it; he would then decide and issue his instructions. General Mladic conceived of the Ministry of Defence so that no one could interfere with the VRS leadership. President Karadzic did not interfere with Bogdan Subotic's work, nor did he interfere in the work of the government presided over by Professor Djeric. General Bogdan Subotic did not agree with Mladic's method of leading the army and he could not support it. When he was appointed the minister of defence of BH he created the Law on Defence and the Army. The duties of the ministry were resolutely regulated by this law with all the necessary explanations. The state administration functioned pursuant to the constitution, laws and regulations and instructions that were resolutely worked out immediately after the formation of the Republika Srpska. General Mladic was in charge of strategic operations. President Karadzic always consulted colleagues on all matters proposed. No decisions were made without consulting the Assembly. From 1993 they had good communications and received daily reports. President Karadzic received his information from three different directions, from the army, the police, and state bodies, municipalities. The government in Pale did its best to ensure the rule of law and response international humanitarian law in 1992. Communication was poor until 1993 and the situation improved only after that. General Bogdan Subotic disagreed with the way General Mladic conducted the affairs and commanded over the army. General Mladic was pigheaded, stubborn, and self-obsessed. He did not care much about others' opinion. He was a narrow-minded sort of soldier. General Subotic was against the war and the Orthodox commanders did not understand or like him. The military was very single-minded and stubborn with no sense of compromise and this is where the problems occurred. President Karadzic is very religious and is a very humane man. In these situations which were not planned he could not agree with the single-mindedness of certain commanders. In Banja Luka in August 1995, there was a document signed by Generals who did not agree with President Karadzic. It was a petition from the generals saying that they would only obey Mladic. The petition was insubordination. President Karadzic brought an order to dismiss General Mladic, but it was not carried out. The competence and authority of the Ministry of Defence were limited to formations and logistical and political matters. Operation and command were not under the authority of the minister until the end of the war. President Karadzic never issued any document containing the words kill, destroy, burn or slaughter. The army and General Mladic had views that were different from those of the president and the government. He had a very Orthodox view of his objective, that he had to defeat the enemy, force him to capitulate and so on. General Mladic was going for the military victory whereas the state leadership wanted to achieve results through negotiations. When Main Staff was established General Bogdan Subotic encountered his first problem as minister of defence. General Mladic imposed upon the leadership of Republika Srpska that this should be called the Main Staff. Mladic and Karadzic were both commanders. The government and the Assembly allowed General Mladic to assume the role of commander, but there could not be two commanders. President Karadzic did not have effective command and control over the territorial units from April the 1st, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are requested to slow down when reading the summary. So could you start over about from the "... effective command and control ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The government and the Assembly allowed General Mladic to assume the role of commander, but there could not be two commanders. President Karadzic did not have effective command and control over the territorial units from April the 1st, 1992, until the creation of the VRS or on May the 12th, 1992, because the Territorial Defence of municipality staffs organised a protection -- the protection of the Serbian population on their territories, either alone or in co-operation with the JNA that was withdrawing. Many factors contributed to complications between President Karadzic, the state leadership, and the Main Staff of the army. General Mladic attempted every method of denigrating President Karadzic's achievements and work by giving completely false informations -- information about his actions and work. On the 8th of May, at the session of the Supreme Command, General Mladic spoke rudely saying that he was not after power and President Karadzic was not in touch with the population, and that Mladic was always closer to the battles than the president. General Mladic's attitude and conduct were impermissible. On August the 1st, General Mladic told Karadzic that he was not his Supreme Commander. On August the 5th on Belgrade Radio, Mladic stated that he did not recognise any decisions that he was in charge and nobody could replace him. On 15th of September, at a session of the War Presidency of the Krajina municipalities, President Karadzic acknowledged that he bore most of the responsibility, but added that he was not listened to and that his orders were never carried out. He added that citizens were also to blame because they did not want to support any measure against negligence. President Karadzic had great respect for international humanitarian law. Apart from tasking General Bogdan Subotic with preparing the Law on the Army, President Karadzic asked him to study and prepare all of the necessary documents which would bind the Republika Srpska to respect the international law of war in combat. They also had the legal framework for the application of International Law of War. It was mandatory for all commanders to instruct their soldiers on the conduct required in relations -- relation to law or war. Throughout the war the President never wanted to sign any documents regarding armed conflict unless General Bogdan Subotic or other experts confirmed that that document was in full compliance with the legal obligations. President Karadzic never gave any verbal or written orders to kill, slaughter, execute, shoot, burn, or destroy. No crimes were ever planned or permitted by these regulations or anyone's positions. Sanctions were envisaged and applied as soon as a crime was discovered. The Main Staff was responsible for implementing the regulations on the law of war, including the treatment of prisoners. Every soldier in the VRS was informed of these instructions. On 12th of May of 1992, all units were placed under the command of VRS. Paramilitaries were only incorporated into VRS if they had not committed crimes. The military courts were under the purview of the president and investigated all the cases of known violations and issued about 300 judgements, judgements of crimes against the Muslims and Croats. President Karadzic never exerted pressure on military courts or the office of the prosecutor. He never exerted pressure or illegal influence on the judiciary. President Karadzic took appropriate steps within his power to ensure that investigations were conducted into crimes committed by army members, the Republika Srpska police, or individuals against the Bosnian Muslims or Croats. He always asked the prosecutor and the president of Supreme Military Court of the Republika Srpska to provide detailed information and demanded that appropriate measures be taken. He endorsed the absolute independence of the judiciary and recommended that enemy crimes be prosecuted and also the perpetrators from their side be tried. President Karadzic never issued orders to shell Sarajevo. He never prevented or ordered to prevent the supply of the Muslim part of Sarajevo with water, electricity, and humanitarian aid. He always insisted that civilians be provided with conditions for a normal life regardless of their ethnicity. Furthermore, there were frequent power cuts and telephones lines were up and down at the seat of the state authorities in Pale caused by the Muslim side. The international community helped the Muslims a great deal. Equipment, food and weapons were sent to the Muslims. There was much dissatisfaction in the army about it, why it was allowed to happen. There were attempts to speak to the Muslims in Srebrenica, calling them to hand over their weapons, to leave and so on. President Karadzic had no knowledge of any crimes committed against Muslims in Srebrenica in July or August 1995. There was great mistrust between the Main Staff and the president, which is probably why the Presidency received very little information from the military leadership. President Karadzic believed the civilian population should decide of their own free will whether they wanted to stay or leave Srebrenica and that no one must be forced. The population wanted to get out of Srebrenica, and this is also what the Muslims wanted. The Republika Srpska leadership agreed to hand over the airport in Sarajevo to the international community so that humanitarian aid would be delivered to the civilian population in Sarajevo to both Serbs and Muslims equally. Military rule was also necessary because of the strong activity of the paramilitary formation, parastate bodies and institutions and because the legal state bodies and other social subjects were not performing their function in accordance with the constitution, the law, and the agreed defence objectives and did not comply with the decisions of the government and other state authorities. President Karadzic and General Bogdan Subotic were against the introduction of a state of war fearing the misconduct from individuals within the ranks of the army and the government. [Interpretation] That's the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I take it you are going to lead some documents with the witness. Before you do so, Mr. Karadzic, I'd like you to deal with the witness about his career, in particular after he quit the job of minister of defence and what he did after he quit that post, and in particular what he did at the time of 1995, because it's not clear from his statement. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellency. That is precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you briefly tell us about your education and then also about your career.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary military school and then the military academy, then the Command Staff Academy of the Yugoslav People's Army. As a soldier, I worked for the most part in the field of education and training, that is to say at the school centre for armored units and mechanised units where students of the secondary school and the military academy were trained as well as those from officers' schools. I achieved significant results in that field, in the JNA, I after all worked at the school centre for 30 years. I received six state declarations, high-ranking ones at that, also a golden plaque of the school centre of the armoured and mechanised units. My position was that I should carry out all my duties conscientiously and precisely, all the duties entrusted to me by the state. That is also the position I was in in 1991 when Yugoslavia was destroyed, when it was broken up by the international community, because that was a marvelous state of fraternal peoples, but the mighty from the international community and America could not bear that, so they tried to sow discord among us by all means, and that is how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, I'm afraid Mr. Karadzic has limited time. The question was about your education and your career. If you could concentrate on answering the question, please. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I was minister for about a year, I was appointed head of the military office of the President of Republika Srpska and military advisor too. Also, I was the chef de cabinet for decorations of Republika Srpska. It was called the decorations office. That's what the law called it. Then I was appointed chef de cabinet of the Supreme Command. Then I was also appointed chief inspector of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in particular in view of this position that you held as chief inspector of the army, tell us in the briefest possible terms what your duties were and whether you managed to carry that out and why the president needed his own source of information and his own inspection.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: You know what? All armies worldwide, including our own, there is this need to have a military inspector. In all countries there are inspectors who check the work of the army. In our army, during that year while I was minister of defence, a great many things happened, things that people didn't even know about. The president didn't know about it. I didn't. The government didn't know about it. We noticed that, as did the government and the members of parliament, and they were absolutely in favour of appointing me to this position so that I could check on what was going on in the military units. My task was to see whether legal provisions, the law, were being adhered to in the government ministry, Ministry of Defence. I took that task very seriously, and I worked on it very precisely. I was often praised by the Main Staff, too, although to my mind I think they were a bit afraid of that task. However, even they praised me considerably for everything that I had observed that -- also about everything that I indicated to them, and things did improve. Unfortunately, after one year, after what year while I was chief inspector of the army, General Mladic and the Main Staff brought a lot of pressure to bear. They didn't want me to be chief inspector of the army any longer. Obviously, they did not like the truth that I conveyed to the government, the Ministry of Defence, and the president of the state. And I mean -- well, actually, their intention was that they do their -- that they do things their way and that the Supreme Commander and the Supreme Command and the government just have a bit of insight into that, the government least of all, because the government as a civilian organ was not really highly regarded by them. So, in fact, after that, after 1993, the president had no one to get official information from except the information that they provided as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been waiting for the interpretation, that's why. General, sir, now, I'm not going to ask about lack of discipline and things like that. During that year while you were inspector, did you see the army committing any crimes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, nowhere, wherever I went, and I toured the area from Banja Luka, Kupres, Jajce, and those other municipalities out there towards the west. Then I toured in detail the areas of Bijeljina, Sarajevo, and Herzegovina. Nowhere. I did everything. I saw everything, wrote everything down, but I never received any information in writing or verbally that anyone had committed any crimes. I did have information about certain groups, certain criminal groups or individuals did certain things, and I conveyed that to the organs in charge and the Main Staff, too, of course. So for example, there was this specific example, actually, when I had this inspection out there, I mean facing the Muslims in the Bijeljina corps. I wrote that in my statement. That's rather interesting. The Muslim media, that evening when I appeared, when I showed up for this inspection, in their media -- they used very strong language in their media. They said that I came to carry out an inspection, that I would dismiss General Mladic on that day, that I would do this and that and the other thing. They were gloating, which was not true. And there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for these other positions that you held, head of the military office and president's military advisor and head of the decorations office, how long did you actually stay in these positions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Up until the end of the war, until Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: You mean after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, tell us -- tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Does it mean that you worked as an inspector of the army until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said that after 1993, sometime at the beginning of 1993, General Mladic insisted that I should no longer be the inspector, that the inspection is no longer needed because the organs of the General Staff would carry on performing that duty. Unfortunately, he managed to convince the president of the republic to accept that, although MPs in the Assembly were not willing to accept that. However, this is how things happened. As for the other duties, I continued performing them until the end of the war, and I continued being the head of the decorations office even after the war, up until 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that on line 13 I'm not sure whether that was in 1993. I believe that you said "1994."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: You mean the abolishment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember, although I wrote that in my statement. I know that I was there until the end of 1993. I know that for sure. I don't know whether I stayed on for a couple more months in 1994. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is still unclear to me is whether you stayed as an advisor to the Supreme Command until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Until the end the war I remained the advisor of the Supreme Command until the end of the war. Also I remained affiliated with the military office of the president of the republic. If you would allow me, I have just remembered the reason why I was removed from the position as the main inspector of the army was the following: When I had planned an inspection visit in Semberija, I had prepared a team which included two colonels from the Main Staff. They were supposed to help me. However, nobody knew where that inspection was to take place save for myself and the president of the republic, i.e., the Supreme Commander. When I arrived at the border facing Muslims, I was met by the military police of the VRS. They stopped me, and they told me, General, sir, General Mladic ordered that nobody was allowed to enter the zone of combat activities. I answered I'm the main inspector of the army. I have the authorities from the state to do that. And then the commander of the police who first addressed me said, General, sir, my task is to force you to return should you not obey the order. Obviously I returned. I did not want to create trouble. I reported back to Pale and I reported back to the president of the republic and that's when my mandate stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What positions did you hold and until when after I transferred my presidential duties to the vice-president, Professor Plavsic, on the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I remained as the advisor of the President of the Republic, Mrs. Plavsic, and as the head of the decorations office. She had the right to ask for my opinions, those that she deemed necessary to help her with the organisation of the army, the army in general, the decorations and so on and so forth, and I stayed in that position until 2004. In 2004, I was arrested by the SFOR in Banja Luka, and I was remanded in custody in Tuzla for four days. About that I have a special note and a special submission, and I will kindly ask the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to allow me to show you what I have prepared, because for that reason I filed a civil suit in the united -- in America, and I would like this Trial Chamber to accept that document, to look at it, and you decide what you want on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 1D9618 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, General, sir, you mentioned decorations and citations that you received while you were still in the JNA. What about the VRS, were you decorated by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the VRS I received four decorations, but those were not military decoration. Those were decorations for work, for humanity, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you can read on this page? The document has not been translated. What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The title of this document is: "Tortures by the High Representative and my arrest." Your Honours, Prosecutors, Defence counsel, I experienced a major injustice. I was arrested on the order of Paddy Ashdown who forced the president of the republic, Mr. Dragan Cavic, and speaker of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, Dragan Kalinic, in 2004, to find anybody who knew the whereabouts of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is one document we haven't seen before. I'm questioning the relevance of this line of examination. This appears to be part of the matter that the witness proactively wanted to raise in connection with a lawsuit he has going, or something to that effect; in any event, it doesn't appear to have a great deal of relevance to the proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the credibility, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the accused wants to address the witness's -- the credibility of -- fine. If the Court sees it that way, that's -- that's -- I have no problem with that, as with any number of matters the accused raises that the Prosecution considers questionable relevance, it's -- it's -- we're willing to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We discussed this in the proofing with the witness and this does relate to his credibility and to the situation where he was placed on a blacklist by the High Representative, arrested by the international authorities for his connection to Dr. Karadzic. It's something that the Prosecution went into with Mr. Bjelica and other witnesses. So it's an issue that relates to his credibility. We had discussed possibly raising this issue in redirect examination, but given that it's been a matter of a lot of importance to this witness Dr. Karadzic decided to lead it in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll allow the Defence to continue, but briefly. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it was recorded that pressure was put on the president of the republic and the Assembly to look for Radovan Karadzic. Can you tell us just briefly what was the reason why you were arrested and ill-treated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In my statement or in my lawsuit I have described all the details, but let me just tell you in a nutshell. Ashdown put pressure on the president of the republic and on the Assembly -- or, rather, the speaker of the Assembly, and the two of them under that pressure caved in, and they said to us, If anybody knew where Karadzic was that would be General Subotic. I received that statement personally from an American colonel who was the deputy of the then commander of SFOR, Virgil Pecket. In our conversation, he told me later on because he was a professional soldier and he respected me as a general, he told me, Your president and your speaker of the Assembly suggested that to Ashdown. However, all that amounted to nothing, because nothing of that was true. But I can only say that every detail and the tortures that my family and myself experienced can only be seen in movies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Besides your arrest, were they interested in anything else? Were there any other actions with regard to the documents and all other possession of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: My opinion is that everybody knows, everybody saw, because the TV crews were always present. In principle, I am an analyst as a soldier and in general terms. From 1991, I maintained notes about the most significant and most important events at that took place. I continued doing then -- that in the course of the entire war in the Assembly, in the government, at all the meetings that I attended, and I was everywhere. Everybody saw that, TV recorded that. I used my own kind of shorthand to make those notes. Those notes contained dates, names, times, and so on and so forth. Later on I concluded after the four days that I had spent in custody in Tuzla and when I returned on day five, when I returned home, I realised that after I was arrested all those diaries containing taken my note had been taken away. There was a team which descended upon my family house. A hundred people participated in that, as far as I know - later on, Colonel Williams admitted to that - and they had taken away from my house all sorts of things, bag full of things. They also took the 20.000 German marks that I kept in an envelope, and so on and so forth. However, after the war, while I was working in Banja Luka in peacetime, after 1996, I worked in the offices of three presidents of the republic, including President Cavic. In my office I had enough time to copy the most important parts of my notes. I typed them on a computer. As far as I know, Mr. Tieger has those notes because they asked me to e-mail all those notes to the Trial Chamber, to the Court, at least that's what Mr. Sladojevic told me. And that's all true. So far from the year 2004, from the 3rd of March, 2004, when there was an assault on my house, nobody has ever turned up with those diaries of mine. I don't know who took them. Nobody ever requested anything from me, nothing. To this very day I am not aware of their whereabouts. What was important for myself, for my office as a minister and what I did during the war, I noted all the those things, the most important things. I don't know what happened to those notes, who took them away, and so on and so forth. Later on I submitted requests to SFOR. However, they turned me down. They did not admit anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted and I see that it time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not already sufficient what is reflected in the transcript, given that this is not translated? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it is corroborative of his oral testimony. He would like it to be part of the written record, and if we could MFI it and get it translated that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I object, and that has no -- this has no place in -- in our documentary base. The witness explained a matter that I continue to think is of marginal relevance, this kind of anticipated rehabilitation of some sort, but I don't know what this document is, and I don't understand why we're -- I mean it is a voluminous record for good reason, but why we would clutter it with document of this type I can't see. Also, I -- I want to -- well, let's -- let's deal with this one matter at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can the witness corroborate himself would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, documents generated prior to his testimony in court can corroborate a witness even if they're authored by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Corroborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, documents created at an earlier date prior to the witness's testimony can corroborate his in-court testimony, I believe. What weight you would give to that corroboration is another thing but I -- in principle I think an earlier drafted document can be corroborative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So the broad principle is a witness can corroborate him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have lots of letters from witnesses, for example, that they wrote during the war. That is an example of how a witness can corroborate himself by some previously written document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, do you wish to comment on that at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will. I -- I mean, I accept -- I understand Mr. Robinson's point but this is a matter that's not in dispute. The witness raised the matter that he was upset with SFOR officials or with Mr. Ashdown and he took some kind of action. That matter is not particularly in dispute. It was raised apparently to appease the witness who raised some concerns about this, but now this is -- this is an attempt to get before the Court all sorts of allegations, specifically allegations that know nothing about on an untranslated document that really are not relevant to the case. So there are two different matters, Your Honour. One, I do accept the idea that if a witness says, I engaged in this event happening, engaged in this action, here's a document which shows the contemporaneous document from the time that shows I did it, that may have point. But here on this very marginal matter the fact that the witness may have initiated some kind of action is one thing, and it's not particularly in dispute. The details of those allegations apparently as reflected in this document are really irrelevant and not a matter subject to the purported corroboration mentioned by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, as I always understood it, the witness doesn't corroborate himself. He may produce a document which shows consistency. Consistency and corroboration are two entirely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour, and I -- you're right. I was not focusing on the precise term that His Honour Judge Baird was focusing on and I think Mr. Robinson and I both missed that in favour of the sort of the general point of consistency as noted by Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes, there are indeed two different concepts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, we allowed this line of questioning because it may relate to the credibility of the witness. The Chamber is satisfied with what is reflected in the transcript, i.e., his oral testimony. In that sense, this document is unnecessary or irrelevant. We'll not receive it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Given the time -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can raise this matter after we return, Mr. President. It's just a clarification of the record, so I don't need to hold up the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly, I just wanted to clarify a potential ambiguity or lack of clarity in the record. The witness referred to some diaries and notes having been taken by SFOR, and then later on as he was explaining that said, As far as I know Mr. Tieger has those notes. Just to clarify what that is about, it has nothing to do with any SFOR action. When we reviewed one of the submissions of the draft 92 ter statement, we noticed portions that clearly appeared to us to be not from the witness's recollection but to be reflections of something that had been previously recorded which we thought was possibly a diary and inquired of the Defence. At that time, we were told something to the effect that the diary from which it had been taken was no longer with the witness but that he had taken some notes from those materials earlier and that was where the -- those portions of the draft statement had come from, and those notes were sent to us. Most, if not all of those are incorporated in the statement the Court has. But I just wanted to explain how the reference to the Prosecution's possession of those notes came about. And, finally, with respect to the discussion we just had about corroboration and consistency, just to note that I think that reflects a bit of a legal cultural gap between two systems. Mr. Robinson and I discussed it briefly. I think we both consider that in our -- the system that we were trained in, that a document produced by a witness can be used to corroborate that witness. The example I used in that case -- in discuss with him was if a witness testified that there was some damage to my house and I -- and, in fact, I filed an insurance claim in connection with that and then produced the insures claim he had filed, that would be, in our system, corroboration rather than consistency. But in any event, the distinction between those two concepts is not one that was particularly at the forefront of our minds. So I only raise that because I -- I didn't -- I didn't want to undercut Mr. Robinson's submission, and, secondly, because the distinction is not as clearly to me as it was to His Honour Judge Baird and His Honour Judge Morrison. I didn't want to later be seen as agreeing or disagreeing with a concept I couldn't claim to fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. You see, corroboration as we understand it by definition is independent evidence, and if it is to be independent evidence, well, then it follows that it couldn't come from the witness to be corroborated. That is the basic -- the basic principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And not to protract it, but I would say our system would deal with that by identifying the nature of the purported corroboration to determine whether it was, for example, so self-serving as to be deemed not legitimate corroboration or whether the manner in which it was produced was sufficient to give it appropriate weight for corroboration. I may be wrong. I don't want to protract this legal discussion any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I think that's probably where the two systems tend to converge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think it's probably where the two systems tend to diverge, but nevertheless it's tomato and tomato.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any further update, Mr. Robinson, about Mr. Beara's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I spoke with Mr. Nicholls and we are in agreement that we're both asking the Trial Chamber to have the matter scheduled for the 27th of June and we also ask the Trial Chamber not to require Mr. Nicholls to be prepared to cross-examine on that day given the uncertainty of what Mr. Beara is likely to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the matter. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you wanted to add something, but because of time constraints if it's in the document, then it's not necessary, because the Chamber has already announced its decision, and we have enough of your words already that refer to that matter anyway.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer by profession, but, please, this incident by SFOR does concern President Karadzic and myself. I was charged by the High Representative of aiding the hiding of President Karadzic. I proved that this is not correct. It was proved in any case that this was not correct. However, I want to say this: I had a contact and a visit to my house by three Americans from Washington. They asked me mostly to tell them something about where Karadzic was hiding. I, of course, didn't know that, but then they continued. The high-ranking advisor to the CIA director came to me. Of course he did announce his visit by letter, and he brought me a letter without a signature and without an address line, and so I figured out that the letter refers to President Karadzic where they are urging him -- of course he asked me to deliver it. I said, I don't know where President Karadzic is, perhaps he's in the United States. But of course I said, I cannot accept a letter that is not addressed to anyone and that is not signed, you know. So we spoke for a long time in my house, and during that time I wrote a letter to President Bush. My daughter translated it. And I asked that gentleman to take that letter to President Bush, but I did address it, and I also did sign it. And I wrote to him about what was being done in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what his army was doing, and other organs, how they are behaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is why I insisted. Well, that's all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we are going a bit too far. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try to follow the chronology a little bit. Did you know what my position was regarding the response to the call-up in 1991 before there was war in our area but the war was beginning in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Your position was very correct and proper. It is known that the war was started by Slovenia, continued by Croatia, and then it transferred the war to Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are facts, and nobody can deny that. The Yugoslav People's Army, or Serbs from Croatia, Serbs from Slovenia, whoever could, fled to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Yugoslav Army and the people, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was full of people, of soldiers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, we need to be as brief as possible. What was my position regarding the response by our people to the call-up, and how did this stand in relation to the law?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The response was just. You came out in favour of the people organising themselves in order to prevent chaos, that lives had to be saved, neighbourhoods, houses, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General Subotic, I know it is very difficult for you, but for the benefit of us having a correct translation, interpretation, please pause before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. All right. Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 32060.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you remember that we communicated by telephone then in December 1991? Do you remember that I was interested in the situation at the front and the response of our people to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very often in the indictment, and it is being ascribed to me as some kind of sin, that he was in favour of mobilisation, meaning myself. Can you tell us whether this was a violation of the law?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, there was no violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. The first part of the question was leading, but I let it go because it wasn't an issue particularly in dispute, and I also saw that Mr. Sladojevic was trying to caution Mr. Karadzic. The second part, though, making a comment, and clearly indicating to the witness what the accused's concerns are about the matter and then seeking a response that will adequately address the accused's concerns is inappropriate both as leading and as commentary and as even guiding a witness beyond what would normally be found in a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Just a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You need to put a foundational question first, and then please refrain from putting a leading question. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency. I think that I did lay the foundation when I asked him whether he was aware of what my position was on the mobilisation before the war in Bosnia while the war was raging in Croatia. I think that's the foundation. I apologise if it was leading. I can put it to the witness differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, have you looked at this intercept recently?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to say whether my interest and my conduct -- what was my conduct and interest like? Did I have any kind of order in mind?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, you did not. Your -- you were concerned. You were asking what's going on, what is the situation like. I said that these people from Croatia were making a push at Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D3708.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we saw in your document on the 15th of April you made a decision on the establishment of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you able to tell us what that implied? Was there a chief? Was there a single command planned?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was inherited, practically from the former Yugoslavia, the old Yugoslavia. Croats, Muslims accepted their own men and in their own areas according to the laws of Yugoslavia. The same thing happened in those areas where there were Serbs. I couldn't say that there was no intermingling among them and so on and so forth, but simply people organised themselves in the best way they could. Right at the beginning I tried -- there was nothing when I came to Pale on the 8th of April, and then I tried to direct things so that we could do something in terms of organisation. There was no army. The JNA was in withdrawal throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia. And we had to have some kind of force that would need to protect people, ordinary people, households, and so then we made the decision to use the already existing TO organisations, to reinforce them as much as we could, and because they had broken off into parts according to the ethnic principle. We wanted to consolidate that there, and we wanted to do something until the army was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to say if you appointed anyone to be at the head of this Territorial Defence, a chief?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Vidoje was appointed as chief of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of Republika Srpska. He had his own staff. I asked General Kukanjac. I requested that he send me any surpluses that he had, extra officers, people who could do something professionally in the interim until the army was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you have just said is in P5565.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at D5614 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, by appointing this colonel, Vidoje Lukic, was there now a control and central authority established over the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: To a certain extent, but in essence, no. To be honest, I did try, but it was not easy. We did not in the true sense of that word manage to achieve that until the army was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at this document. Could you see who signed it, and could you tell me if you took part in the drafting of this decision?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The government -- the government and myself as the minister of defence in the government. This document was signed by Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the question about this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether the general took part in the drafting of the decision signed by Djeric and whether by appointing Colonel Lukic central control was established over these municipal and other territorial defences that he referred to as being scattered. It was only on the 15th of April that we got some colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3709, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please tell us this: A bit earlier you mentioned this multitude of Territorial Defences. Can you please tell us according to the then national defence law in force at the time, what were the powers of the municipalities in terms of defence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The powers of the municipalities were there. I mean, they had municipal staffs. They had municipal units of the Territorial Defence. All of that was pursuant to the Law of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the found situation at the beginning of April or March or in late 1991 onwards was what was then used in all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to say how this was? What were the autonomous functions of the municipality in relation to defence affairs?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The municipality had its municipal staffs. It had its own units of the Territorial Defence which in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were formed for the purpose of extraordinary situations, emergencies, and this was under the laws of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did this reflect in our conditions in 1991 to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the only kind of organisation, that initial phase, the only organisation that provided any kind of security to the population, that people will not be able to do whatever they wanted and that anybody would be able to attack whoever they wanted. There was some sort of safety or security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, who was it that was supposed to pay the reservists who were registered in the TO of some municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: That was the duty of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did it actually make the statements in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a symbolic payment, not right at the beginning, though, but around that time. Until the army was formed there was some kind of symbolic, minor compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what would the powers of the municipalities in terms of salaries for their brigades?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This went through the municipal TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please look at 65 ter 18709. This is the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in -- dated the 13th of June, 1992. Could we please now look at page 15. 7500, that's the ERN number. I believe that's page 15. And what we can see here is we can see your -- actually, my and your order for the respect of international law. It seems that this is not translated. This is 206.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That addendum which you signed, you can see the signature in the right-hand column. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We do not see this on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lower left-hand corner, 206.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said we do not have a translation for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 65 ter. The Prosecution did that, but it's not translated. Perhaps it is, but I don't see that it is. If we have 206 translated, then all the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, why don't you collapse the English version and zoom in on the B/C/S. Yes. 206.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what it says here: [As read] "Rules on the level and way of payment of compensation to members of the reserve force of the army who haven't been included in establishment units of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina until now." So that is the heading. And now Article 1, and could you please focus on Article 2 now. That would be the top of the right-hand corner. It says here: [As read] "The resources for compensations referred to in Article 1 of these rules shall be ensured as subsidies to budgets of municipalities that municipalities will plan as separate items. Payments and control of resources shall be ensured by the organ of defence of the municipality on the basis of records that will be provided by the command and the units of the army."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Dr. Karadzic. He started speaking too fast after he stopped reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Subotic. The interpreters were not able to catch up with your speed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, yes, the units of the army. So it's the question that wasn't interpreted. Can you tell us until when this kind of financing of municipal units through municipal budgets went on and whether volunteers were treated equally? I mean, how did this reflect on volunteers that were part of municipal units?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, this lasted up until the end of the year approximately, and volunteers in these municipal units were treated equally. I mean, together with these reservists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, Article 206?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3710, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was a state of war proclaimed briefly, for a short period of time, end of June 1995? Do you remember what the powers were of the War Presidencies in respect of mobilisation and other things that were done in relation to defence?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This is the powers that they had. All the population that was available, except for those who were involved in some work obligation and for the very bare necessities of functioning, I mean, they were supposed to respond to call-up, to mobilisation, because we had this critical situation in the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D44042 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember this document that you issued? Actually, can you read it? The text, not the part up there.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Commissions established on the basis of the order of the president of the republic, number 01-1120/95, dated the 16th of June, 1995, for checking mobilisation shall complete their activities on the 30th of July, 1995, because the decision on the declaration of a state of war gave these powers to the War Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. Can you tell us about this stamp? What does number 2 mean within the stamp?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Number 2? The president of the republic had stamp number 1, and the head of the military office had stamp number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the establishment of the military judiciary was within whose authority? Can you tell us whether you worked on that? Can you tell us about the problems you had to resolve just briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: That was within your authority as the president of the republic, and I as your assistant and head of your military office was given certain tasks regarding organisation, then preparing sessions and preparing other documents, that is to say, everything that you as the president of the republic did not have enough time to do. That is to say I carried out all of those preparations. Then they came because you called them, and then we resolved these problems together, and that is the way things went until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have and to what extent investigation organs and experts, and so on? What was it that you found there and how did this develop?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. You gave me the authority to find professional judges all over Republika Srpska in agreement with the Ministry of Justice and so on, also to find pathologists and experts who could assist military courts in resolving crimes and carrying out other professional work in that regard. There are documents to that effect and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D44040.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We see here, I mean, this decision say for a military conscript. Dr. Branko, medical centre in Banja Luka. He is appointed a medical expert in the field of pathology. That is to say that I had the authority, in agreement with the Ministry of Justice and so on, and through consultations, et cetera, to admit him, I mean into the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude towards crimes committed by Serbs against Muslims or Croats? What kind of instructions did people have, say this military pathologist, in terms of the ethnicity of the victims or perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Very precise instructions, that's what they had. And I really insisted up to a maximum that this should be precise, accurate, timely, and so on. So I never allowed -- well, maybe you also remember this from debates and sessions that we had with the military judiciary and so on, then also with the minister of justice together. We always insisted that all of this had to be done on the basis of regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of cases when experts like this one or investigators, military investigators, the military judiciary or military prosecutor and so on, that they hushed up or concealed something?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not aware of any such case. I certainly would have been informed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3712, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I just mention it wasn't particularly a problem here, although it could have been. If we could just have a -- a -- some summary indication of what the document is before the witness explains it. That was a bit lacking, but the witness's explanation I think allowed us to understand it sufficiently, but I'm concerned with other documents that may be more of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you have any insight into the situation the beginning of 1992, before the outbreak of the conflict? Did you know to what extent the SDS could control processes on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, in part I did have insight because, I mean, I had, I mean, my own organs of the Ministry of Defence and all municipalities, and so on. And I got that from them because they worked with the members of the party and so on. This was a single system of work. All of that functioned on the basis of those instructions that we had, I mean, that were prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for rising, but I think there is an ambiguity that is significant here. The question was about the beginning of 1992 which I normally take to mean around January or February. The witness is answering in the context of his arrival in Pale after April as I understand it, so if the -- if the colloquy continues I think we have a built-in ambiguity. I think we need to know specifically what time period we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could clarify with the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, within the JNA was there information about the situation on the ground, and from that point of view did you have reports about the attitude towards -- or, rather, the participation of political parties in developments before the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In part, yes, I did, I mean. Well, not everywhere, not in all areas. But, I mean, where I functioned, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D44034. Could we please have that displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, this was signed by Radislav Mitrovic from the command of the 7th Operations Group, and could you please look at line -- or, rather, paragraph 3. Are you familiar with such documents and this kind of information? It says up here, "Information provided by."

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This text is barely legible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the top of the page, the command of the 7th Operations Group, the 19th of February, 1992, information provided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, please, are you familiar with this? Was this customary? Are you familiar with such an information? How often did they circulate through the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of some but not all. For example, this one, from the command of the 2nd Military District, I did know about this, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to ask you to look at the second -- no, third paragraph in the 1st Military District, a telegram arrived signed by Milan Babic, and the JNA's required to leave Krajina, and SDS extremists are spreading an alarmist campaign and announcing the establishment of their own army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question or answer. We were doing a sight translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the SDS in Croatia, Babic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear your question in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The SDS, is this the SDS in the Serb Krajina within Croatia? Is that what is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, no. In Krajina, in the Croatian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe the Court is not having the difficulty I am in following the colloquy, but it does seem to implicate the concern I raised before where we're immediately into a document on the basis of a question about whether or not the witness had any familiarity with information being about -- through the JNA about the situation, a question so broad as to encompass anything and not provide any assistance. Now we're talking about a particular document about which we know nothing because we have no translation, and we're -- we're focusing on particular parts as if there's some understanding of what that document in general is. It's difficult to know where the questions are going, what they're relevant to without at least some indication and understanding of what the document is, and I think in the past we've operated on that basis, at least an indiction of what we're looking at before we get into the details. It also has implications in terms of leading but more importantly just in terms of simple comprehension we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The heading says the 7th operation group, but the witness said from the command of the 2nd Military District. So I tend to agree with Mr. Tieger's observation. We have little information about what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you help us with this? What kind of document is this -- or, rather, documents that circulated in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. On the other page. On the second page. Could we see the second page? Could we see who this was sent? My mistake I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's a leading question as well, whether it was circulated throughout -- in the JNA or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this information was sent to, General? It says so on this page.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This information was sent to members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kind of information is this? What does it speak of?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It speaks of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sent by who? That's a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see the first page. Could we enlarge the signature so the general could see who this is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mitrovic, Mitrovic, but I don't see this, the name, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read his position and rank.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale and, I don't know, some kind of affairs. So, in fact, this was -- as we say, this was the military ideologue in the 7th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go pack to page 2 and then page 3? What is this document? Is this the first time you see it -- or, rather, is there something unusual here or is it the usual type of document, and what is it by its nature?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: In terms of its nature, it is propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how does it portray the situation on the ground, falsely or correctly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Falsely. No, falsely. This is a document that I see before me, and it presents the situation falsely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at page 3 now so that we see how they portray the situation in Bosnia. So just in Bosnia, down there we see the Serb Krajina. Can you read this to yourself and then see -- THE PROSECUTOR: The witness did not answer the question about whether or not it was the first time he saw the document which I think is significant since he's characterising it as false and now being asked to address portions of the document which he may or may not have seen before. I think it would be useful to have an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, have you seen this ever, and are you familiar with this type of information that are sent out in the field?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I saw this information, and I am familiar with this type of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As Mr. Tieger properly indicated, when we do not have the English translation, it's difficult to follow the witnesses answer, whether -- when he says this is false or not or not. So please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, it says here the latest developments in BiH, the second paragraph. Could you read it out.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes: "The recent developments in BiH confirm that the SDS is not in full control over the situation either. Some local leaders and extremists objectively inflict damage on the Serb people there."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear Mr. Karadzic's because we were finishing the sight translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Subotic, please pause. Please pause. And, Mr. Karadzic, you as well, please pause. Please repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this paragraph fit into your own knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: This paragraph absolutely reflects an illogical position that is detrimental for the Serb people. It's as if it were written from Croatia, from some Communist ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber something about the relations between the SDS and this type -- this profile of JNA officer and also in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: JNA officers who came to Republika Srpska and who were in Republika Srpska otherwise, who happened to be there, who were Orthodox Communists, they did not attach any importance to political parties. Croatian officers, to Croatian political parties, Bosnian officers to Bosnian parties, Serb officers to Serb parties. They only knew one thing, I mean, one ideology. That was Titos, and those were the views they expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I tender this document, Excellencies? Do you need it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Subotic, what I find it difficult to follow is this: You said this is written by a Mitrovic in the 7th Tactical Group to be circulated to JNA members for propaganda purpose. I don't follow. Who was Mitrovic, and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mitrovic is an ideologue in this 7th Tactical Group. Political Commissar, if we can put it in army terms. He didn't like something there, because he was still living in the clouds and he did not realise what was happening in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And then he tried to -- well, in terms of people who were protecting Yugoslavia, who wanted to protect the people, I mean, didn't work. That is what this Mitrovic is trying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And is a -- is the 7th Tactical Group a part of JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 7th Tactical Group, that is part of the JNA. That doesn't mean that all members of this Tactical Group thought the same way as this Mitrovic did. We in the Army of Republika Srpska also had quite a few "komesars" whose views differed from the views of the entire Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI 3713, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please help us. In one paragraph of your statement you mentioned that the Islamic religious community was involved in the arming; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN SUBOTIC
